title: How to Analyze Bank Stocks (Part 1): Leverage, Accounting, and Loan Losses
summary: Eisman builds bank analysis from accounting, leverage, capital rules and credit provisioning, then argues current bank credit is stable while private-credit warnings may appear elsewhere first. His leverage arithmetic and core CECL timing are useful. The audit corrects the deposit-multiplier framing, exclusive reliance on risk-weighted regulation, rating-agency delegation, Tarullo title/date and CECL history. Some absolute statements confuse uncertain estimates with necessarily wrong accounting, and conditional identities with real-world causation. Current stability does not settle future private-credit risk.
assessment: The strongest material is explicit leverage and loss arithmetic, with assumptions retained. Historical and regulatory simplifications require substantial correction. Neither accounting changes nor later stock appreciation prove management motive or a guaranteed contrarian investment outcome.
speaker_map_notes: The sole SPEAKER_00 self-identifies as Steve Eisman and delivers the full tutorial.
framework_points: Read accounting as a test of the business narrative.
Separate return on assets from leverage-driven return on equity.
Stress loss absorption using capital and asset exposure.
Compare risk weights with actual underwriting changes.
Separate loan growth provisions from deterioration provisions.
Watch credit recognition lags and indicators outside bank statements.
tools_and_charts: Hypothetical $1 billion-equity banks at 1,10 and 100 times leverage
Large-bank CET1 table from Q4 2024 to Q2 2026
Major-bank nonaccrual table across Q2 2025, Q1 2026 and Q2 2026
transcript_cautions: Captions repeatedly substitute ROA for ROE: the 100% return at 100 times leverage is ROE, while assumed ROA remains 1%. The surrounding arithmetic resolves the intended identity; no separate false ROA forecast is created.
The compensation sentence says ROE versus ROE; adjacent explanation clearly contrasts ROA with ROE.
Cecil is CECL, chewing up istrueing up, and Tarula is Tarullo.
A JPMorgan stock price appears as $84 million; this is not accepted literally, and the price-date comparison remains unverified.
Chip accounting is called semiconductor profits even though depreciation concerns users of capitalized chips; no issuer is specified.
The four-bank nonaccrual chart itself is absent from the transcript.
